title: AARO, 2022 to now
notes: Start-here flag 5. A connector hub: claims sourced to it cap at Tier 2 unless about what it said.

lead.text: AARO is the Pentagon office created by a Deputy Secretary of Defense memorandum of 15 July 2022 as the Department's authoritative office for UAP. Its reports and its director's testimony say it has found no verifiable evidence of extraterrestrial technology, while its director also concedes a residue of cases the office cannot explain.

summary.text: The founding memorandum makes AARO the Department of Defense's authoritative office and focal point for UAP, covering anomalous space, airborne, submerged and transmedium objects. It orders the UAP Task Force disestablished and its data and materials transferred to AARO, supersedes the AOIMSG direction of 23 November 2021, and places the office under the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security.

Congress gave the office its legal identity: its authority and annual reporting duty are codified at 50 U.S.C. 3373 through the FY2022 and FY2023 NDAAs, and sec. 6802 requires a joint DNI and Secretary of Defense annual report, limited to five reports, and a written report on the historical record.

Three people have run it: Sean Kirkpatrick from its establishment to 1 December 2023; Tim Phillips, Deputy Director on assignment from ODNI, as Acting Director from December 2023 to August 2024; and Jon Kosloski from August 2024. After Grusch testified in summer 2023, Deputy Secretary Hicks moved the office out of the USD(I&S) chain so that its director reports to her directly.

Its public output is three consolidated annual reports, Volume I of the Historical Record Report, explanatory information papers and a small video release channel. In 2026 the larger PURSUE release ran through the Secretary of War's website, with AARO identifying and staging the material rather than publishing it.

record.text: The FY2023 report, the first statutory annual report, logged 291 new reports (274 from the period, 17 from 2019 to 2022) and 801 total holdings as of 30 April 2023. It said only a very small percentage of reports show interesting signatures such as high speed or unknown shapes, and it made no finding of any kind on extraterrestrial technology.
The FY2023 report names its own blind spot: the space and maritime domains still had to be fully integrated into AARO's processes, since 290 of the 291 reports were airborne.

The FY2024 report records 757 reports received, 485 from the period and 272 from 2021 and 2022 not in earlier reports, and 1,652 in total as of 24 October 2024. It is also where the standing sentence on no evidence of extraterrestrial beings, activity or technology first appears.

The FY2024 report says AARO posted historical documents on KONA BLUE, which it describes as a prospective and not approved Special Access Program brought to its attention by interviewees who claimed it was a DHS compartment to cover up the retrieval and exploitation of non-human biologics.

The FY2025 report rests on 50 U.S.C. 3373k, covers 2 June 2024 to 30 May 2025 and was published on 21 July 2026, months late. Its cover reads Department of War where the FY2024 cover read Department of Defense. It again rejects claims that the government holds recovered UAP material while saying AARO is writing procedures for handling such material should any come into government possession.
The FY2025 report's section on foreign partners is two sentences long and names no foreign office, air force or archive, only a briefing by AARO's deputy director at a conference in London.

Kirkpatrick was the sole witness of record at the Senate Armed Services Emerging Threats and Capabilities subcommittee hearing of 19 April 2023, chaired by Gillibrand and printed as S. Hrg. 118-648, which followed a closed session the same day. He testified that AARO was investigating more than 650 cases and that spherical objects made up nearly half of reports.

Kosloski's statement for the record at the Senate hearing of 19 November 2024 puts AARO's holdings at over 1,600 reports and says the office has discovered no verifiable evidence of extraterrestrial beings, activity or technology. It does not mention whistleblowers, Immaculate Constellation or Volume II of the Historical Record Report.
AARO's case slides at the same hearing assessed the GO FAST object at about 13,000 feet and 45 mph in 60-knot winds, concluding it showed no anomalous speed or flight characteristics.

AARO's September 2025 information paper states that the office cannot declassify anything on its own: it must ask the originating offices for review, and DOPSR reviews redactions before release. The paper says classified imagery protects platform capabilities, locations and collection methods, so even footage of ordinary objects stays classified when it comes from sensitive sources.

AARO's own imagery page released seven numbered clips between 4 December 2025 and 6 January 2026, all European incidents from 2021 to 2024. One was resolved as almost certainly birds, one was judged insufficient for a determination, and the rest were left unresolved. The same page says GO FAST, GIMBAL and FLIR remain unresolved.

In May 2025 AARO issued a Sources Sought Notice for a custom case management system hosted on JWICS, which on the board's record shows the office had no purpose-built case system three years after it was set up.

AARO contracted Oak Ridge National Laboratory in 2022 to test a magnesium alloy specimen. Volume I's magnesium-zinc-bismuth finding and the ORNL magnesium and aluminium analyses are the only physical-specimen work AARO has published.

Volume I commits AARO to a Volume II. It was deferred by the Pentagon in August 2024, promised within months by Kosloski in November 2024, scheduled for late 2025 in a June 2025 departmental statement, and had not appeared as of August 2026.
AARO's homepage carries banners for PURSUE, linking to war.gov/UFO, and for UAP records at the National Archives, directing the public to channels it does not run.
AARO disclosed its GREMLIN prototype sensor platform for real-time UAP data collection at the Volume I rollout in March 2024.

claimed.text: Kosloski told senators in November 2024 that AARO does have some very anomalous objects and does not believe every object is a bird, a balloon or a drone. He described unresolved cases including a very dark object near a large orange sphere that accelerated vertically, and a stationary cylinder near a facility in the southwestern US that disappeared.

Grusch testified under oath that he had a classified conversation with Kirkpatrick in April 2022, before Kirkpatrick took over AARO, and raised concerns with him. Kirkpatrick has not publicly denied the meeting.

Jake Barber said on a January 2025 podcast that the Michael Herrera incident was presented to AARO under Kirkpatrick, who denied it, and that Kirkpatrick later privately confirmed it to Senate Intelligence Committee members. This is Barber's account of what Kirkpatrick is said to have said in private; no record of either the denial or the private confirmation has been opened.

Former Senate staffer Kirk McConnell said on a podcast that the contract for an advisory group Kirkpatrick formed at AARO was let through Oak Ridge, and that Kirkpatrick now works for Oak Ridge under contract. He called it worth noting and does not allege wrongdoing.

Skinwalker Ranch owner Brandon Fugal said Kirkpatrick claimed never to have attended a briefing on the ranch, and that Kirkpatrick in fact sat across from him at a confidential briefing on it in April 2018; Fugal says he then published a photograph of Kirkpatrick in attendance.
Witnesses at the House hearing of 9 September 2025 testified that AARO holds unreleased UAP video. That testimony became the stated basis for Luna's 2026 demand for videos.

Luna, who chaired that hearing, called Kirkpatrick a documented liar and AARO's channel a graveyard for testimony. After meeting Kosloski in May 2026 she said he had apologised for prior leadership's conduct and that the earlier office had been set up to block and suppress information; the apology itself has not been published.

contested.text: Kirkpatrick argued in Scientific American, seven weeks after leaving AARO, that the crash-retrieval narrative is circular reporting from a small group of people traceable to Robert Bigelow and AATIP, and that whistleblowers who seek public attention rather than bring evidence to AARO are suspect. The board notes the op-ed advanced the frame of the office's own Volume I before it was published.

Kirkpatrick said after the July 2023 hearing that the central source of the allegations had refused to speak with AARO. AARO's own memorandum records Grusch declining nine interview approaches; Grusch cites legal and security exposure. Both facts sit in the same document.

The board infers that the no-evidence formula is a communications response rather than an analytic finding: the FY2023 report has no extraterrestrial-technology denial, and the FY2024 report, the first after the Grusch hearing, leads with one.
The FY2025 report contradicts itself on satellite flaring: one section says 44 events were resolved as flaring, while the executive summary and another section say a new capability resolved 238.

Volume I states AARO found no non-disclosure agreements containing UAP information; the Department later confirmed that Air Force personnel signed NDAs over a fictitious alien-technology programme, the Yankee Blue matter, which AARO reportedly uncovered under Kirkpatrick. A Pentagon spokesperson could not confirm the department-level memo described in the press.

Neither AARO's annual reports nor its director's statement for the record addresses Immaculate Constellation, a programme name entered into the Congressional Record, and Kirkpatrick has publicly denied that it exists.

On the board's reading, the declassification paper's account of a slow, fixed process was overtaken within eight months by its own department, which cleared five tranches and over a hundred sensor videos once directed at cabinet level; the board also reads AARO's seven clips as minimum compliance.

Kirkpatrick went from AARO to Oak Ridge National Laboratory as its chief technology officer for defence and intelligence programmes, the laboratory that performed AARO's specimen analyses. The post-employment question has been raised publicly and never adjudicated; the board records the link for proximity, not impropriety.

The board infers that an office without subpoena power or independent counsel, reporting to the deputy head of the department that would own any concealed programme, cannot structurally resolve concealment allegations, which is why every AARO denial is worded as what AARO has not discovered.
The chair of the 2026 UAP Science Advisory Council, Avi Loeb, co-authored a paper with Kirkpatrick while Kirkpatrick directed AARO.

questions: What was said in the April 2022 conversation between Kirkpatrick and Grusch, and did Kirkpatrick document it?
Which companies did AARO visit, and did it have any power to inspect contractor holdings, or rely on voluntary corporate statements?
Was AARO given access to waived or unacknowledged special access programmes when it assessed its cases?
Why has Volume II of the Historical Record Report not been published, who decided to defer it, and does a draft exist?
What exactly did Kosloski say to members of Congress in May 2026, and was he consulted on the design of PURSUE?
Did Oak Ridge receive AARO's material sample before or after any recusal arrangement covering Kirkpatrick?
Why did AARO's GO FAST analysis not address why a 2015 fleet safety warning about the same video was recalled?
